raw_text:
{{RunningHeader|troubadour|6502|trough}}of early poets who first appeared in Provence, France. {{smaller|The troubadours were considered the inventors of a species of lyrical poetry, characterized by an almost entire devotion to the subject of chivalric love, and generally very complicated in regard to meter and rime. They flourished from the eleventh to the latter part of the thirteenth century, principally in the south of France, Catalonia, Aragon, and northern Italy. The most renowned among the troubadours were knights who cultivated music and poetry as a polite accomplishment; but the art declined, and in its later days was chiefly cultivated by an inferior class of minstrels. See ''trouvère''.}} '''troublable†''' (trub′la-bl), ''a.'' [ME. ''troublable'', < OF. *''troublable'', < ''troubler'', trouble: see ''trouble'' and ''-able''.] Troublesome; causing trouble; vexatious. {{smaller block|Lecherie tormenteth hem in that oon syde with gredy venims and ''troublable'' ire. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boethius, iv. meter 2.}}}} '''trouble''' (trub′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''troubled'', ppr. ''troubling''. [< ME. ''troublen'', ''trublen'' (also transposed ''turblen''), < OF. ''troubler'', ''trubler'', ''trobler'', also ''tourbler'', ''turbler'', ''torbler'', F. ''troubler'', trouble, disturb, < ML. *''turbulare'', < L. ''turbula'', disorderly group, a little crowd of people, dim. of ''turba'', crowd (> ''turbare'', disturb), = Gr. τύρβη, disorder, throng, bustle (> τυρβάζειν, disturb): see ''turbid'', ''turbulent'', and cf. ''disturb'', ''disturble''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To stir up; agitate; disturb; put into commotion. {{smaller block|An angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and ''troubled'' the water. {{right|John v. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|A woman moved is like a fountain ''troubled''. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., v. 2. 142.}}}} '''2.''' To disturb; interrupt or interfere with. {{smaller block|We caught here a prodigious quantity of the finest fish that I had ever before seen, but the silly Rais greatly ''troubled'' our enjoyment by telling us that many of the fish in that part were poisonous. {{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 312.}}}} '''3.''' To disturb in mind; annoy; vex; harass; afflict; distress; worry. {{smaller block|Thou didst hide thy face, and I was ''troubled''. Ps. xxx. 7.}} {{smaller block|The boy . . . so ''troubles'' me 'Tis past enduring. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 1. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Not so sick, my lord, As she is ''troubled'' with thick coming fancies, That keep her from her rest. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 3. 38.}}}} {{smaller block|This great Tartarian Prince, that hath so ''troubled'' all his neighbours, they alwayes call Chan. {{right|''Capt. John Smith'', True Travels, I. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|He was an infidel, and the head of a small school of infidels who were ''troubled'' with a morbid desire to make converts. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xix.}}}} {{smaller block|Nothing ''troubles'' social life so much as originality, or political life so much as the spirit of liberty. {{right|''J. R. Seeley'', Nat. Religion, p. 140.}}}} '''4.''' To put to trouble, inconvenience, pains, or exertion of some kind: used conventionally in courteous requests: as, may I ''trouble'' you to shut the door? {{smaller block|Your master's a right honest man, and one I am much beholding to, and must very shortly ''Trouble'' his love again. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, v. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|I shall ''trouble'' you to give my services to my friends at Oxford. {{right|''Arbuthnot'', in Letters of Eminent Men, I. 180.}}}} {{smaller|'''To cast oil on troubled water.''' See ''water''.=''' Syn. 3.''' ''Afflict'', ''Distress'', etc. (see ''afflict''); perplex, agitate, plague, pester, badger, disquiet, make uneasy, anxious, or restless.}} II. ''intrans.'' 1†. To become turbid or cloudy. {{smaller block|Put a Drope of Bawme in clere Watre, in a Cuppe of Sylver or in a clere Bacyn, . . . and ȝif that the Bawme be fyn and of his owne kynde, the Watre schalle nevere ''trouble''. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 52.}}}} 2. To take trouble or pains; trouble one's self; worry: as, do not ''trouble'' about the matter. {{smaller block|We have not ''troubled'' to shade the outside of this diagram. {{right|''J. Venn'', Symbolic Logic, p. 281, note.}}}} '''trouble''' (trub′l), ''n.'' [< ME. *''trouble'', ''truble'', ''trubuil'', ''torble'', ''turble'', < OF. ''trouble'', ''tourble'', trouble, also a crowd, F. ''trouble'', trouble; from the verb.] 1. Vexation; perplexity; worry; difficulties; trials; affliction. {{smaller block|Man is born unto ''trouble'', as the sparks fly upward. {{right|Job v. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|When we might be happy and quiet, we create ''trouble'' to ourselves. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 205.}}}} 2. Annoyance; molestation; persecution. {{smaller block|For "Ioseph shulde dye" playnly dyd they say, But pacyently all theyr ''truble'' dyd he endure. {{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}}}} {{smaller block|Tyre alone gave those two powerful princes, Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander the Great, more ''trouble'' than any other state in the course of all their wars. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. 84.}}}} 3. Disturbing, annoying, or vexatious circumstance, affair, or state; distress; difficulty. {{smaller block|To take arms against a sea of ''troubles''. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1. 59.}}}} {{smaller block|What was his ''Trouble'' with his Brother Geoffrey but a Bird of his own hatching? {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 53.}} Fears concerning his own state had been the ''trouble'' with which he had hitherto contended. {{right|''Southey'', Bunyan, p. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''trouble'' about owning a cottage at a watering-place is that it makes a duty of a pleasure. {{right|''C. D. Warner'', Their Pilgrimage, p. 193.}}}} 4. A source or cause of annoyance, perplexity, or distress: as, he is a great ''trouble'' to us.—5. Labor; laborious effort: as, it is no ''trouble''. {{smaller block|Is twenty hundred kisses such a ''trouble''? {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 522.}}}} {{smaller block|Insomuch as they have not dared to hazard the revenue of Ægypt by sea, but have sent it over land with a guard of Souldiers, to their no small ''trouble'' and expences. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 40.}}}} 6. In ''law'', particularly ''French law'', anything causing injury or damage such as is the subject of legal relief.—7. A disease, or a diseased condition; an affection: as, a cancerous ''trouble''.—8. In ''mining'', a small fault. Also called a ''throw'', ''slide'', ''slip'', ''heave'', or ''check''. = '''Syn. 1-3.''' {{smaller|Inconvenience, embarrassment, anxiety, adversity, misfortune, calamity, sorrow, tribulation, misery, plague, torment. See the verb.}} '''trouble†''', ''a.'' Same as ''troubly''. '''troubledly†''' (trub′ld-li), ''adv.'' In a troubled or confused manner; confusedly. {{smaller block|Our meditations must proceed in due order; not ''troubledly'', not preposterously. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Divine Meditation, xvi.}}}} '''trouble-house†''' (trub′l-hous), ''n.'' [< ''trouble'', ''v.'', + obj. ''house''1.] A disturber of the peace of a house or household. {{smaller block|Ill-bred louts, simple sots, or peevish ''trouble-houses''. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 53.}}}} '''trouble-mirth''' (trub′l-mėrth), ''n.'' [< ''trouble, v.,'' + obj. ''mirth.''] One who mars or disturbs enjoyment or mirth, as a morose person; a killjoy; a spoil-sport. {{smaller block|But once more to this same ''trouble-mirth,'' this Lady Varney. {{right|''Scott,'' Kenilworth, xxxvii.}}}} '''troubler''' (trub′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''trouble'' + ''-er''1.] One who or that which troubles or disturbs; one who afflicts or molests; a disturber. {{smaller block|Let them . . . hurl down their indignation
On thee, the ''troubler'' of the poor world's peace! {{right|''Shak.,'' Rich. III., i. 3. 221.}}}} '''trouble-rest†''' (trub′l-rest), ''n.'' [< ''trouble, v.,'' + obj. ''rest''1.] A disturber of rest or quiet. {{smaller block|Foul ''trouble-rest,'' fantastik greedy-gut. {{right|''Sylvester,'' tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, ii., The Furies.}}}} '''troublesome''' (trub′l-sum), ''a.'' [< ''trouble'' + ''-some.''] 1. Annoying; vexatious: as, a ''troublesome'' cough; a ''troublesome'' neighbor. {{smaller block|''Lord Plausible.'' I wou'd not have my Visits ''troublesome.''
''Manly.'' The only way to be sure not to have 'em ''troublesome'' is to make 'em when People are not at home. {{right|''Wycherley,'' Plain Dealer, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The Arabs and people of the country are civil enough, and shew it in their way, by coming and sitting about you; tho' they are ''troublesome'' by being too observing, curious, and inquisitive. {{right|''Pococke,'' Description of the East, I. 181.}}}} 2. Difficult; trying: as, a ''troublesome'' shoal or reef; a ''troublesome'' fellow to deal with. {{smaller block|I beshrew him for his counsel! there is not a more dangerous and ''troublesome'' way in the world than is that into which he hath directed thee. {{right|''Bunyan,'' Pilgrim's Progress, i.}}}} {{smaller block|The Rais said he had a design to have anchored there last night; but, as it was ''troublesome'' to get out in the morning by the westerly wind, he intended to run over to Perim island to pass the night. {{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 311.}}}} 3. Tumultuous; turbulent; boisterous. {{smaller block|There arose in the ship such a ''troublesome'' disturbance that all the ship was in an vprore with weapons. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. 1. 111.}}}} {{smaller block|When cloudless suns Shine hot, or wind blows ''troublesome'' and strong. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Naming of Places, vi.}}}} 4†. Troublous; disturbed. {{smaller block|In the ''troublesome'' times 'twas his happinesse never to be sequestred. {{right|''Aubrey'', Lives (Francis Potter).}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn.''' 1 and 2. Harassing, wearisome, perplexing, galling.}} '''troublesomely''' (trub′l-sum-li), ''adv.'' In a troublesome manner; vexatiously. {{smaller block|He may presume and become ''troublesomely'' garrulous. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxiv.}}}} '''troublesomeness''' (trub′l-sum-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being troublesome. {{smaller block|The lord treasurer complained of the ''troublesomeness'' of the place, for that the exchequer was so empty. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''trouble-state†''' (trub′l-stāt), ''n.'' [< ''trouble'', ''v.'', + obj. ''state''.] A disturber of the community; a disturber of the peace. Also used attributively. {{smaller block|Those fair bates these ''trouble-states'' still use (Pretence of common good, the king's ill course) Must be cast forth. {{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, III.}}}} {{smaller block|Soul-boiling rage and ''trouble-state'' sedition. {{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 14.}}}} '''troublous''' (trub′lus), ''a.'' [< ''trouble'' + ''-ous.''] 1. Agitated; disturbed. {{smaller block|As a tall ship tossed in ''troublous'' seas,
Whom raging windes, threatning to make the pray
Of the rough rockes, doe diversly disease. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ii. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|The street shall be built again, and the wall, even in ''troublous'' times. {{right|Dan. ix. 25.}}}} 2. Restless; unsettled. {{smaller block|His flowing toung and ''troublous'' spright. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|Some were ''troublous'' and adventurous spirits, men of broken fortunes, extravagant habits, and boundless desires. {{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 501.}}}} 3. Disturbing; disquieting. {{smaller block|They winced and kicked at him, and accused him to Ahab the king that he was a seditious fellow, and a ''troublous'' preacher. {{right|''Latimer'', Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}} {{smaller block|My ''troublous'' dream this night doth make me sad. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 2. 22.}}}} '''troubly†''' (trub′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''troubly'', ''trowbly'', ''trobly'', ''trubyly'', ''trouble'', ''trowble'', < OF. ''troublé'', ''troblé'', pp. of ''troubler'', ''trobler'', trouble: see ''trouble'', ''v.''] 1. Turbid; stirred up; muddy; murky. {{smaller block|In Ethiope alle the Ryveres and alle the Watres ben ''trouble'', and thei ben somdelle salte, for the gret hete that is there. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 156.}}}} {{smaller block|These fisheris of God shulden . . . not medle with mannis lawe, that is ''trobly'' water. {{right|''Wyclif'', Select Works, I. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|A ''trouble'' wyne anoon a man may pure. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 201.}}}} {{smaller block|Thei loked towarde lanneriur, and saugh the eyr ''trouble'', and thikke of duste. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 236.}}}} 2. Troubled; confused; distraught. {{smaller block|It may fall sumtyme that the ''trubylyere'' that thou hase bene owtwarde with actyfe werkes, the mare brynnande desyre thou sall hafe to Godd. {{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 31.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''trowbly'' erroure of oure ignoraunce. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boethius, iv. meter 5.}}}} 3. Turbulent; tempestuous; stormy. {{smaller block|The ''trowble'' wynde that hyht Auster. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. meter 7.}}}} '''trouflyng†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''trifling''. '''trough''' (trôf), ''n.'' [< ME. ''trough'', ''trogh'', ''trou'', < AS. ''trog'', ''troh'', a trough, a small boat (''trohscip'', ''trochscip'', a cock-boat), = D. ''trog'' = OHG. MHG. ''troc'' (''trog-''), G. ''trog'' = Icel. ''trog'' = Dan. ''trug'' = Sw. ''tråg'', a trough; cf. It. ''truogo'', a trough, < Teut.; lit. 'a thing of wood,' or perhaps 'a log' (sc. hollowed out); from the root of E. ''tree'', AS. ''treów'', etc.: see ''tree''. Cf. ''trow''2, ''trogue'', and ''tray''1.] 1. An open receptacle, generally long and narrow, as for water. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A wooden receptacle or basin in which to knead dough.}} {{smaller block|She lifted the mass of dough out of the ''trough'' before her, and let it sink softly upon the board. {{right|''Howells'', Annie Kilburn, xiv.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') A large vessel, usually oblong, designed to hold water or food for animals.}} {{smaller block|One meets everywhere in the roads [of Switzerland] with fountains continually running into huge ''troughs'' that stand underneath them, which is wonderfully commodious in a country that so much abounds with horses and cattle. {{right|''Addison'', Remarks on Italy (Works, ed. Bohn, I. 519).}}}} {{smaller block|(''c'') A conduit for rain-water, placed under the eaves of a building; an eaves-trough. (''d'') In ''printing'': (1) A water-tight box in which paper is dipped to dampen it for the press. (2) The iron or metal-lined box in which inking-rollers are cleaned and forms are washed. (''e'') In ''fish-culture'',}} a hatching-trough. 2†. A small boat; a canoe or dug-out. {{smaller block|If none had proceeded further then the inuentions of our predecessors, we had had nothyng in the Poets aboue Andronicus, and nothing in histories aboue the Annales or Cronicles of Bysshoppes, and had yet haue sayled in ''troughes'' or in boates. {{right|''R. Eden'' (First Books on America, ed. Arber, p. xlviii.).}}}} {{smaller block|There is a great caue or ditch of water . . . where come every morning at the break of day twentie or thirtie canoas or ''troughes'' of the Indians. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', III. 454.}}}} 3. A concavity or hollow; a depression between two ridges or between two waves; an oblong basin-shaped hollow: as, the ''trough'' of the sea. {{smaller block|Where the ''trough'' of one wave coincides with the crest of another, if that crest be equal, the resultant motion at that point is null. This is the result of the mutual interference of waves. {{right|''A. Daniell'', Prin. of Physics, p. 129.}}}} 4. The array of connected cells of a voltaic battery, in which the copper and zinc plates of each pair are on opposite sides of the partition.—5. In ''chem.'', a vat or pan containing water over which gas is distilled.—6. In ''electroplating'', a tray or vat which holds the metallic solution. ''E. H. Knight.''—{{smaller|'''Glass trough.''' (''a'') A deep and narrow box of clear glass for holding objects for microscopic study in their natural liquids. (''b'') A similar device for holding the developing or fixing bath in dry-plate photography, in order that the changes in the plate submerged in the bath can be observed.—'''Pneumatic trough.''' See ''pneumatic.''—'''Trough of barometric depression,''' an advancing area of low pressure, the line of places, lying transverse}}
